# Relays and Distribution

A **relay** receives content from a publisher and forwards it to subscribers. It moves the copying work off the publisher's connection, allowing the same publication to reach more viewers.

How does one copy from the lecturer become a copy for every student? We’ll follow the relay’s subscriptions, look at what it caches, and see how it handles viewers with different connection speeds. We’ll also look at which jobs need other parts of the service.

## How does a relay share content? {#a-relay-plays-both-roles}

The relay subscribes to the lecturer’s content, then publishes it to the students. It has a separate connection on each side and reads the MoQ messages to decide what to forward.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A relay shares one source among several viewers
  accDescr: The publisher sends one audio track to a relay. The relay sends a separate copy to Alice, Bob, and a recorder.
  P["Lecturer publishes audio"] -->|One upstream copy| R["Relay"]
  R --> A["Alice"]
  R --> B["Bob"]
  R --> C["Recorder"]
```


With several interested viewers, a relay can share upstream content and forward it to each downstream connection. If a second relay is closer to another audience, it can repeat that pattern. A network of these relationships provides distribution across regions.

Each downstream connection still needs its own bytes. For one 2 Mb/s track and 100 viewers, the difference looks like this. These figures count payload only, before transport overhead.

| Distribution | Lecturer sends | Relay sends | Each viewer receives |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Lecturer connects directly to every viewer | 200 Mb/s | — | 2 Mb/s |
| Lecturer sends one copy to a relay | 2 Mb/s | 200 Mb/s | 2 Mb/s |

Here, the lecturer uploads 2 Mb/s and the relay sends 200 Mb/s across its viewer connections. With more relays, we can do the same calculation for each link.

### Can subscriptions reduce encoding work too?

Suppose the lecturer offers high- and low-resolution video, but every viewer chooses the lower resolution. Forwarding only that track saves network traffic. Avoiding the unused high-resolution encoding can also save work at the publisher.

The moq.dev [concepts guide](https://doc.moq.dev/concept/) describes how subscriptions carry demand back to the publisher. An application using its library can start an encoder for the first subscriber and stop it after the last one leaves. A recorder counts too, so closing every player may still leave someone receiving the track. The application has to implement this behavior; MOQT doesn’t control the encoder.

There’s a startup cost to consider. When the first viewer asks for an idle rendition, the publisher needs to start encoding and send the configuration and a picture the viewer can decode. Until then, that viewer has to wait.

## What does a relay need to know? {#relays-need-structure-not-codec-knowledge}

A relay uses names, group boundaries, priorities, and delivery rules. It need not inspect the encoded picture to forward it. That separation makes a generic relay useful for audio, video, and application data.

For this to work, the publisher needs to put the right media at each group boundary. Suppose the relay sends a new viewer a group that depends on pictures from the previous group. The relay has delivered what was requested, but the player still can’t show it.

## How does caching help new viewers? {#caching-helps-but-has-limits}

A caching relay can hold recently received objects. A new viewer may obtain a useful group without waiting for the original publisher to send it again. An object is identified by its full track name, group ID, and object ID within a scope. Its payload cannot change, allowing different viewers to reuse the same cached bytes. Some object properties can change under their own rules; immutability does not apply to every cached field.

How much history is available depends on the relay. [MOQT allows caching](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-7.1), and each relay decides what to keep within its memory budget. A viewer joining late needs to find out whether the objects it wants are still there.

For the lecture, retaining a few useful recent groups may improve startup. Keeping the entire class for replay is a separate storage feature with different costs and lifetime requirements.

## How does delivery differ between viewers? {#each-hop-has-its-own-conditions}

The lecturer’s connection can be fast while one viewer’s connection is slow. A relay has to make downstream delivery decisions for each path. Slowing every viewer to match the slowest one would defeat the point of independent subscriptions.

Alice’s connection may deliver each new group immediately, while Bob’s connection builds a queue. Their playback delay differs even though both request the same publication. The relay can choose delivery settings for each subscription according to that viewer’s path.

Measure at the edges, then trace through the hops. A healthy publisher-to-relay connection says little about a congested relay-to-viewer connection.

## Which jobs belong to the wider service? {#what-a-relay-does-not-automatically-do}

Suppose a student needs low-resolution video, but the publisher only sends high resolution. Someone has to create the smaller version. A **transcoder** does that by decoding and re-encoding the media. The service might run one alongside a relay, which then forwards the resulting objects.

The service also has to choose nearby relays, connect them, and recover when one fails. The moq.dev project includes clustering features to help with this setup.

Before scaling the lecture, draw the actual publisher, relay, and viewer paths. Mark where content is cached and where authorization is checked. That small drawing often reveals more than a single “CDN” box.
